body_text: Sweetgreen is in a tough spot. The premium-priced slop bowl seller has recently been caught in a vortex of rising labor costs, increasing wholesale food prices, and choppy sales. The company is eager to be known as something other than the place that sells $20+ salads. Instead, the Wall Street Journal reports that Sweetgreen is eager to be known as the place with the $15 wraps. The company is also beefing up portion sizes and making build-your-own salad pricing more transparent in an effort to woo customers. Perhaps the only people more dejected by Tuesday’s election results than Republican politicians are data center developers. Data centers – the kilowatt-sucking warehouses filled with server racks and cooling equipment – were on the ballot across the country and the results were emphatic: Voters don’t like data centers. They really really don’t like data centers. In the 41 local races across the country where a data center moratorium, new regulations, or a specific project itself was on the ballot, voters weighed in against data centers 40 times, Semafor reports . Those election night results don’t come out of the blue, of course. Back in May, Gallup found that 71% of Americans opposed data center construction in their area. To put that 71% opposition figure in context, building new data centers is just about as unpopular as releasing the Epstein files is popular ( 75% of Americans support the latter.) In terms of the market reaction to voters’ data center displeasure, it would be easy to look at the post election rally in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 and think that meant that investors expected little to no hiccups in the AI trade, and specifically, the data center trade, to proceed with little to no hiccups while Democrats control the House and Senate. Looking a bit more granularly at the market reaction, that doesn’t seem to be the case. While the broad indices are indeed up, the VanEck Semiconductor ETF and the RoundHill Memory ETF – which as their names indicate, respectively track semiconductor and memory storage shares – ended the day in the red. Nvidia , Broadcom , and Marvell all tumbled. (In a sign of just how negative investor sentiment is, AMD printed strong earnings and boosted guidance and ended the day barely eking out a gain.) And who among the AI trade gained on the day? The hyperscalers – Amazon , Google , Meta , Microsoft – were all in the green. SpaceX was conspicuously down, as investors reassessed the downsides of Elon Musk’s close alliance with the President Trump and the failure of Musk’s interventions on behalf of the GOP in Texas’s statewide races. What investors are saying, in a sense, is that if right now you have an already operating data center, it just got more valuable . And if your business is selling stuff to build not-yet-existing data centers, that business just got on balance a little less profitable going forward. As Bloomberg’s Joe Weisenthal put it , the “[Meta Hyperion] campus in Louisiana might be able to charge some pretty high rents.” The massive data center build out in recent years across the Sun Belt in particular was done in large part with full industry enmeshment with the national and state Republican party. That strategy will now largely be unavailable. However, in a purely analytical way – dare we mention game theory ? – despite the tables being fully turned, that strategy had a certain logic. Indeed, if you were in charge of a hyperscaler or an AI lab with an interest in seeing data centers getting built, being as close as possible to Trump and the GOP may have made sense. Assuming a blue wave was coming and there was nothing really that you could do about it, Trump and the GOP were the path to getting the most compute online while you could. Any data center that wasn’t already up and running on Monday has a lower chance of becoming operational and a longer lead time with higher costs if it does. The challenge that the entire data center and AI industry must now reckon with is the blue wave did indeed happen, and Democrats will (accurately!) view their anti-data center campaign messaging as key in helping them win. An industry not used to oversight or much, if any, national-level regulation will now be a key regulatory and investigation target of a party emboldened by a historic win. When you think of the company that Steve Jobs founded some 50 years ago , your mind likely first arrives at the various devices that have truly revolutionized the way we live in the modern world, of which the company now says there are 2.5 billion in active use globally. However, Apple’s Services division — often the source of those just-small-enough-to-dismiss transactions that leave your account each month, with various cloud and content subscription payments tacked on to give users the full run of Apple’s walled garden — has become a huge part of the pie, with revenues reaching yet another record in the company’s fourth quarter. In Q4, sales from Services reached a whopping $31.57 billion, up some 9.8% from the same period last year. While that might have snapped a double-digit growth streak that had run for 12 quarters in a row, as analysts quoted by Variety observed, it still means that Apple offerings such as TV+, Music, Pay, Podcasts, News+, and others are raking in more than $13 billion more each quarter than they were five years ago. The difference between how much profit Services takes in compared to Apple’s main cash cow, the Products segment, also speaks for itself: The cost of sales on the whopping $82.9 billion that Products brought in for Q4 was $52.1 billion, while the Services segment's cost of sales for the same period was just $7.6 billion. While slowing growth and the unending popularity of Apple’s devices — the company this week said it’s unsure whether it will be able to get more iPhone Duos in by the all-important Christmas trading period, after the $2,000 foldables sold out in a matter of weeks — might mean Services will never catch up to Products in the amount of cash they generate for the company, the profit race between the two has been getting more interesting. title: 🗳️ Trading the midterms
body_text: If you’ve ever eaten a potato but wished you’d roasted a chicken, well, do American food scientists have just the foodstuff for you. It took food scientists at Cornell University more than a decade, but the Poulette – a potato that tastes like chicken – has arrived, Food and Wine Magazine reports . The quest to develop this specific new tuber began with chef Dan Barber’s love of heirloom vegetables (seriously, as someone who once sat through about a dozen courses of different kinds of obscure squash at Blue Hill at Stone Barns, I can say the guy is obsessed with the stuff), and in this case a specific type of French potato that was then crossed with a more modern varietal by researchers. The Poulette is sold by Barber’s seed company and will be available in (of course) Whole Foods’ locations in the tri-state area. Today is Election Day in the United States, and traders will be keeping a close eye on the returns to get a sense for how the partisan makeup of Washington and, in some cases more crucially, governor mansions may change for the next two years. First things first, what is likely already priced in. As it stands, prediction markets have a 94% chance * that Democrats take control of the United States House of Representatives and a 76% chance of taking the Senate . While everyone’s model is a bit different, on balance traders have been likely positioning themselves for split control in Washington, with Democrats controlling Capitol Hill and Republicans the White House. As Sam Ro points out, “the periods before and after midterm elections are famously volatile for stocks,” Markets tend to perform well once there’s a clear indication of a result, and in general equities catch some tailwinds once the uncertainty is in the rearview. In yesterday’s EntryPoint , Luke Kawa put it succinctly: “History says that just getting the midterms out of the way will be a positive for US stocks.” However, options markets have been essentially treating the midterms as a non-event. After all, with such a high chance that the House flips, at this point a divided government in Washington can be considered highly likely regardless of the outcomes of a few massive Senate races. Now, that’s not to say there’s nothing on the line here for traders. One concern coming from some analysts on the Street is that, with the midterms in the past and the risk to his coalition realized, President Trump will lose one potential reason to not escalate the politically unpopular war with Iran. That’s more a matter of timing than the actual results, though, but if I run an airline I’m not exactly looking forward to the next couple of weeks of fuel cost price action. What will be watched very closely by anyone involved in the AI trade is the performance of a number of candidates who have been riding a wave of anti-data center enthusiasm that has cut across traditional party lines . For instance, while markets still currently price her as a 37% underdog in Texas against incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott, Texas Rep. Gina Hinojosa has called for an immediate moratorium on data centers. Texas has more large projects underway than any other state , and that’s been motivating voters who oppose the projects regardless of their typical politics. A win for Hinojosa would likely have ramifications for the AI trade on Wednesday, given the Lone Star state has 27 GW of data center capacity planned; wins for adversaries of the data center development across the map would likewise constrain the ability of the hyperscalers to, well, hyper scale. Polls close at different times over the course of the evening, and states tend to count votes at different speeds from one another. Some states have speedier counts and can expect their votes to be counted super quickly — Florida, after a rather infamous 2000 election, got its house in order and is now one of these — while some states are going to take some time, like Maine, which reports by township and thus will be slow to provide results. By looking at key congressional districts in states that report quickly and close early, we’ll have some indications pretty early in the evening as to how the election is likely to play out over the course of the night. It’s not perfect — the voters in Michigan and the voters in Texas will likely behave similar in general, but have enough differences that we’re not expecting a uniform swing across the map — but if you want some early insight as to how the race is going to go, here’s a few early races that election projection decision desks like DDHQ are going to be paying attention to: The first instructive polls close at 7pm, and Florida and Virginia will be the fastest to report. Look to Virginia’s 1st and 2nd District , Florida’s 15th and 25th for how the House might go. If Democrats flip VA-02, they’re on track for a good night, and if they flip VA-01 as well or hold both Florida districts the Democrats are very likely to flip the House. If Republicans flip the Florida districts, or manage to hold VA-02, they could very well hold the House. After 8, we’ll get results in Ohio and North Carolina. The bellwether districts in North Carolina are NC-01 and NC-11 , keep an eye on those for an indication of how the night will go. If there’s a call in Ohio’s Senate race for the Democrats, they’re then the favorite to flip the chamber. Just because we’ll have some strong hunches early in the evening doesn’t mean we’ll have precious clarity any time soon. With a close Senate race in Alaska that (a) won’t start posting results until after midnight Eastern Time and (b) will go to a ranked-choice instant runoff if no candidate clears 50%, it’s entirely possible that we don’t know control of the Senate by opening bell on Wednesday.
